newsitem.title: USA: Three years of litigation led to tobacco settlement.
newsitem.headline: Three years of litigation led to tobacco settlement.

text.p: The historic tobacco industry settlement announced Friday comes as the industry faces hundreds of individual and class-action lawsuits in U.S. civil courts.
Here is a chronology of some recent major developments:

April 14 - Heads of seven leading tobacco companies confidently deny to Congress that nicotine is addictive, ushering in what would become known as the "third wave" of tobacco litigation focusing on the addictive nature of nicotine and allegations the tobacco industry manipulates the level of nicotine to keep smokers hooked.

May 23 - Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore becomes the first state legal officer to sue the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. Eventually about four-fifths of the nation's top legal officers will join the battle.
Nov. 28 - U.S. Supreme Court refuses to block a lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. and two advertising agencies on whether a Camel cigarette advertising campaign improperly targets minors.

Dec. 12 - Dade County, Fla., Judge Robert Kaye agrees to certify Norma Broin vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al, as a class action. The lawsuit, the first class action for alleged health problems caused by secondhand smoke, seeks damages on behalf of 60,000 flight attendants who say they were sickened by secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

July 24 - UST Inc.'s United States Tobacco Co. and other smokeless tobacco companies are sued in U.S. District Court in Wichita, Kan., for allegedly promoting their products to teenagers and hiding the addictive nature of nicotine.

Aug. 10 - A day after President Bill Clinton announces regulatory steps to cut youth smoking, five major U.S. cigarette manufacturers file suit against the FDA seeking to block its attempt to regulate cigarettes.

Aug. 22 - Philip Morris and R.J. Reynolds Tobacco say they settled multibillion-dollar libel suits against ABC-TV for a 1994 broadcast alleging the tobacco companies manipulated the amount of of nicotine in cigarettes. ABC settled the suit by apologising for a report on its "Day One" news magazine.

Dec. 4 - Lawyers for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. ask federal appeals court to allow them to pursue a civil lawsuit against Merrell Williams, a former paralegal assistant who copied company documents and then sold them to anti-tobacco lawyers. The documents would be widely published.

Feb. 6 - Jeffrey Wigand, former research chief at Brown & Williamson and tobacco industry whistleblower, sues his former employer for invasion of privacy. Wigand had appeared on a television show on Feb.4 accusing the company of using cancer-causing additives in its cigarettes, lying about the addictive nature of nicotine and other wrongdoings.

May 23 - Federal appeals court throws out the "Castano case," a nationwide class-action lawsuit that threatened to pit millions of smokers against tobacco companies, agreeing with industry's contention that such cases should be tried individually. Lawyers return to court one day later to file amended lawsuit and promise to file additional lawsuits in most of the 50 states and U.S. territories.

May 28 - U.S. Supreme Court rejects appeal by five tobacco companies and two tobacco trade groups of a ruling that required them to turn over to Minnesota extensive computerized databases in connection with Minnesota's 1994 lawsuit against tobacco companies seeking to cover the costs of providing medical care to indigent and uninsured smokers.

August 9 - Jacksonville, Fla., jury slaps Brown & Williamson with a $750,000 judgment in a liability case filed by Grady Carter of Orange Park, Fla., who was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1991. The tobacco industry defeat, which it appealed, was its first since a jury in 1988 awarded $400,000 to the family of Rose Cipollone of New Jersey. The 1988 award was overturned on appeal.

Aug. 23 - Clinton formally approves new federal oversight measures regulating tobacco, which, among other things, require proof of age to purchase cigarettes, ban cigarette sales through vending machines in areas accessible to teenagers and ban tobacco advertising near schools.

Jan. 24 - New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco files first suit against the tobacco industry seeking the dissolution of two of its research groups, alleging they are merely a publicity front for cigarette makers.
Feb. 7 - A federal judge rules that a Massachusetts state law requiring tobacco companies to disclose the ingredients in their cigarettes is valid.
March 13 - Mississippi Supreme Court rules that the first state Medicaid suit seeking to recoup health care costs of smokers can go to trial.

March 20 - Breaking ranks with the industry, Liggett Group reaches settlement with 22 state attorneys general to end lawsuits aimed at recouping health care costs of smokers. The accord calls for unprecedented concessions from Liggett that include turning over secret documents that could hurt the entire tobacco industry.

April 16 - Several state attorneys general say tobacco executives had begun negotiating for the first time in early April with states on a possible settlement of massive litigation against the industry.
April 25 - U.S. District Court Judge William Osteen in Greensboro, N.C., upholds the Food and Drug Administration's authority to regulate cigarettes as a drug delivery device.

April 27 - U.S. Supreme Court rejects a constitutional free speech challenge and allows cities to ban billboards that advertise cigarettes or alcoholic beverages in public places frequented by children.

May 5 - A Jacksonville, Fla., jury clears R.J. Reynolds Tobacco of responsibility for the death of Jean Connor, a smoker who died of lung cancer. Connor's family was represented by Norwood "Woody" Wilner, the attorney who scored the almost unprecedented victory in the Carter case.

May 12 - South Carolina adds its name to list of states suing the tobacco industry to recoup money spent treating Medicaid patients with smoke-related illnesses. It is the first major tobacco-growing state to join the effort.

June 2 - Jury selection begins in Miami in class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of 60,000 non-smoking U.S. flight attendants who say they became ill from breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on passenger jets. It becomes both the first secondhand smoke and first-class action suit against big tobacco to make it to trial.

Friday, June 20 - Tobacco companies agree to pay $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and their advertising as part of a landmark agreement. In return, the companies, would be given immunity from any further punitive liability for deception, fraud or conspiracy that might have occurred in the past.
